The plaintext is an original passage written for this puzzle.  The ciphertext in
examples/ratchet-challenge.txt is that passage enciphered with the key below; the
app prints the letters-only form, so the hash is taken over letters only.

The published crib is 150 letters from the middle of the message, at offset
4066 of the 6778-letter stream:

    NEANARCHIVETHATMINTSITSDOCUMENTSWITHARATCHETISTRUSTINGEVERYCLERKEVERYDUPLICATEEVERYQUOTATIONANDEVERYCITATIONTOKEEPQUIETFOREVERWHICHISAVERYLONGTIMETOAS

The crib attack is exact either way -- every letter of the message comes back,
including the part before the fragment (the state map the equations pin is
relative; only the message's first letter is out of reach).

  * with the offset named, `--hint crib_offset=4066`: about 1.4 s
  * without it, sweeping every offset: about 29 s

The ciphertext-only route works too, which is what makes this challenge a fair
one either way.  Measured on this container with four workers and a real budget
rather than a slice:

  * the engine, exactly as the app runs it -- `buttcrack crack --file
    examples/ratchet-challenge.txt --budget 300 --workers 4`: solved, confidence
    1.00, in 107 s
  * the attack on its own, same budget: exact reading in 111 s

The command line also follows the crib route end to end: with the fragment above
and `--hint crib_offset=4066 --budget 90` it reports the reading in about 33 s,
of which the ratchet attack itself takes 1.3 s (the rest is the collection the
engine tries first, on the way to the cipher that declares the hint).

A note on the key the attack reports, which is worth knowing before you compare
key strings.  The interval sums leave the *value axis* free: any unit u mod 26
composed with a shift s -- 12 x 26 = 312 keys -- deciphers this ciphertext to the
identical message (verified: all 312 do, from the second letter on), and only the
publisher's own key deciphers a *different* message.  On this challenge the attack
returns the publisher's key gauged by u = 7, s = 0: a different key string that
deciphers the same ciphertext to the same plaintext.  Compare the plaintext, or
the hash, and not the key.

plaintext (letters only, as the app reports it)
    

plaintext (as written, with layout)
The archive keeps a ratchet on its door, and the ratchet keeps a secret of its own.

A ratchet is the oldest piece of engineering that nobody notices. It is a wheel with teeth, a pawl that rides those teeth, and a promise: the wheel turns one way and not the other. Wind a clock, tighten a strap, raise a drawbridge, and the same three parts do the work. Nothing about the mechanism is clever. What is clever is what the mechanism permits, and what it permits is accumulation.

An archive is an accumulation. Every letter filed is one click of the wheel, and the wheel does not go back. The shelf grows, the catalogue grows, and the dust grows with them. A reader who walks in on Monday finds a different room from the one a reader found on Sunday, though no single object has moved more than a shelf.

Cryptographers borrowed the ratchet early and never returned it. A running total is the same idea in a different costume: begin at nothing, add one measured quantity for each step, and let the total stand for the step. A bank ledger, a pedometer, a tide gauge, a scoreboard, a mechanical odometer, half the clocks ever built. All of them say the same sentence, which is that the present is the sum of everything that has happened so far.

Consider how much of secrecy is patient addition. A courier carries a number, and the number was made by adding a long column of smaller numbers that only the sender knows. The receiver does not need the column. The receiver needs the total, and the right to subtract. Secrecy of that kind is not a wall but a tally, and it is defended less by the strength of any single figure than by the arithmetic that ties one figure to the next.

The weakness of a ratchet is exactly its virtue. The one-way promise is a promise about order, and order is precisely what a patient opponent learns to read backwards. Give a mathematician a long enough list of totals and the increments come back one by one, because each total is the previous total plus something, and the something is what the adversary wants.

Suppose you are handed a page of ordinary text in which every letter has been replaced by the reading of a wheel that turns one click for each letter of the message. The top row of the wheel is a cipher alphabet. The bottom row is a second cipher alphabet, and the click moves the bottom row along by one, so that the letter just written now leads the row it was read from. It is a charming machine to watch. It is also a running total wearing two rows of letters, because the reading of the wheel at any moment is the sum of the plaintext's positions since the start, relabelled through the bottom row.

Nothing on the page tells you where the wheel stood when the message began, and nothing tells you which letter of the alphabet occupies which tooth. The letters look flat and evenly spread, as a good polyalphabetic cipher's should, and the counts of single letters, of pairs and of triples all look like the counts of a random shuffle of the same letters. A few hundred characters of that page will keep their secret for a very long time, and no amount of quick counting will dent them.

Then a fragment of the message arrives from somewhere else. A quotation that was quoted in a letter, a ledger entry, the name of a ship, a line of a will, a sentence somebody repeated in another document entirely. Whoever holds that fragment holds a key, and the key does not have to be long. Sixty letters would embarrass the machine. A hundred and fifty would end the argument.

The reason is the interval sum, and the interval sum is the whole of the trick. Find two positions in the ciphertext that show the same letter and look at what the wheel did between them. It stood somewhere. It clicked forward with every plaintext letter in between. It arrived back where it started. Therefore the positions of those plaintext letters on the top row of the wheel, added together over the interval, must come to nothing. That is one linear equation in the twenty six unknown positions of the top row, and every other pair of equal letters in the ciphertext writes another one.

An enemy with a fragment of known plaintext can write down hundreds of these equations and solve them, not over the ordinary integers but modulo twenty six, which is to say over a small clock of twenty six hours. The arithmetic is not even hard. It splits into a problem on the two hour clock and a problem on the thirteen hour clock, each of which is a plain exercise in elimination, and the two answers are stitched back together by a rule the Chinese knew long before the wheel was invented. When the equations are done, the few positions the fragment never touched are filled in by trying the handful of possibilities and reading the result aloud. The message falls open like a book that was only ever held shut by habit.

So the ratchet is a poor way to keep a secret and an excellent way to keep a record. It hides the letters and not the length of the walk. Anyone who can guess one sentence of the message, or who owns a copy of it in another drawer, can recover the rest without ever having seen the machine. An archive that mints its documents with a ratchet is trusting every clerk, every duplicate, every quotation and every citation to keep quiet forever, which is a very long time to ask of a filing cabinet.

The archives of the last century are full of ratchets that were believed to be walls. Mechanical counters with secret starting positions. Diplomatic codebooks whose additions were thought to be the hard part. One time pads that were never one time. A sculpture on a lawn in Virginia whose first three sections sat unread for decades and whose last section is still a rumour. In every case the weakness was not the amount of secrecy. It was the fact that the same secrecy was reused, and reuse is the ratchet's whole design.

What survives is the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is friendly. A cipher that accumulates is a cipher that can be undone by anyone willing to write down what accumulated. The wheel is beautiful, the mechanism is honest, and the sum is patient. In the end the archive always tells you more than it intended to, which is why the archive is worth keeping.

A pawnshop keeps its secrets the same way. Two alphabets stand side by side on the counter, and the merchant reads one against the other with the confidence of a man who has done it a thousand times. The first alphabet is what the documents say. The second is what the documents mean. Anyone who learns to slide the two along each other owns the shop, and that is the whole of cryptanalysis in a single gesture. The ratchet is the slide that never stops sliding.

There is a lesson here about noise floors, which is the phrase an engineer uses for the smallest signal worth believing. A short message made with a moving wheel is all floor and no signal. Its letters are too evenly spread to measure, its differences too few to count, its intervals too sparse to close into equations. A few hundred letters of such a message are genuinely safe, and every handmade challenge of that size that has ever been posted to a forum is safe with them. Which is why the challenges that get solved are the ones that arrive with a hint attached, or with a second copy in another drawer, or with somebody who quotes a line of the letter in the next paragraph of the story.

Length is the cure and the disease. Three thousand letters of English prose carry roughly as much language as a paragraph of a newspaper, and the statistics of a moving wheel begin to be visible in them, the way a face becomes visible in a photograph taken in poor light. Ten thousand letters carry the shape of the language itself, and a patient attack can then measure the differences of neighbouring letters three letters deep and find the one relabelling of the alphabet under which those differences read as English. The wheel does not care about the meaning of the message. It only cares how long the message runs, which is a strange thing for a lock to care about and a very ordinary thing for an archive to provide.

The message you have just read was written for a puzzle. It was enciphered with a wheel whose two rows are both mixed alphabets, one click per letter, and its ciphertext travels with a single published fragment of its own middle. If you are reading it as plaintext rather than as evidence, then the wheel has been turned back, the equations have been solved, and the ratchet has kept its last secret for the day.
